title: Translation Studies
author: Susan Bassnett
src: Bassnett, S. (2014). Translation Studies (4th ed.). Routledge.

sections.h: A discipline in its own right
p: The name Translation Studies was proposed by André Lefevere in 1978 for the discipline concerned with ‘the problems raised by the production and description of translations’. Bassnett’s aim is to show that it is a field of its own, not a corner of comparative literature or linguistics.

Translation has long been treated as secondary and ‘mechanical’, and critics have judged products without studying the process. Bassnett traces this low status to the 19th-century ‘servant-translator’. Rossetti called the translator’s work self-denial; FitzGerald boasted of taking liberties with the Persians, ‘who really do want a little Art to shape them’. Both positions fit the colonial hierarchies of the time.

The old quarrel over whether translation is an art, a craft or a science is beside the point. The real need is a shared terminology for studying it. Levý: a translation is ‘an interpenetration and conglomerate of two structures’. Catford (1965) separated substituting TL meanings for SL meanings from transferring SL meanings into the TL.
list: History of Translation: theories over time, critical reception, commissioning and publishing, single translators (product).
Translation in the TL culture: influence of texts, authors and genres, and the norms of selection (product).
Translation and Linguistics: comparing SL and TL from phonemes to syntax; equivalence, untranslatability, machine translation, non-literary texts (process).
Translation and Poetics: literary translation in theory and practice, by genre (poetry, theatre, libretti, film dubbing and subtitling) (process).
sections.note: Evaluation is culture-bound: there can be no definitive translation, any more than an ultimate poem or novel. A translation can only be judged by its process and its function in a given context.

sections.h: Language and culture; Jakobson’s three types
p: Translation has a linguistic core but belongs most properly to semiotics, the study of sign systems. Sapir: no two languages represent the same social reality, and ‘the worlds in which different societies live are distinct worlds, not merely the same world with different labels attached’. Lotman: language is the primary modelling system, and art and literature are secondary ones.
Bassnett’s image: language is the heart within the body of culture. A surgeon cannot ignore the body around the heart, and a translator treats a text in isolation from its culture at their peril.
list: Intralingual translation (rewording): other signs in the same language.
Interlingual translation (translation proper): signs of another language.
Intersemiotic translation (transmutation): non-verbal sign systems, such as film, music or painting.
sections.note: Jakobson: there is ordinarily no full equivalence, even between synonyms (perfect/ideal, vehicle/conveyance), so poetry is technically untranslatable and only ‘creative transposition’ is possible. Mounin’s example: English pastry is not Italian pasta, whatever the dictionary says.

p: Nida’s model sees translation as analysis, transfer and restructuring. Even ‘yes’ and ‘hello’ are not simple. French has oui and si (si contradicts); Italian and German often string affirmatives (sì, sì, sì), which sound comic in English. Italian pronto is only for the telephone, while ciao means both hello and goodbye. The translator isolates the invariant (affirmation, greeting) and replaces the sign: Ludskanov’s ‘semiotic transformation’.

Butter and Italian burro name the same product, yet British butter is yellow, salted, spread on bread and high-status (‘bread and butter’), while Italian burro is pale, unsalted and used for cooking. Each language is a separate reality. Words like ‘spirit’, with many senses, depend on context and make puns possible.

Situation-bound phrases (Say when; Bon appétit) are translated by function. For a father’s ‘Bon appétit’ breaking a tense family silence, the translator must: (1) accept that it is linguistically untranslatable, (2) accept that English has no such convention, (3) weigh the possible phrases (Dig in, Tuck in, Do start, I hope you like it) against speaker, status and setting, (4) weigh its weight in the scene, (5) replace the invariant core in both the text’s system and the culture’s.
sections.note: Levý held that leaving out difficult expressions is immoral: the translator must find a solution. The translator is not the author of the source text, but as author of the target text has a clear moral responsibility to its readers. Neubert: ‘Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?’ cannot be rendered semantically where summers are unpleasant.

p: Idioms are swapped by function, not by image: Italian menare il can per l’aia (‘lead the dog round the threshing floor’) becomes ‘beat about the bush’. Dagut: a metaphor is new, so an equivalent cannot be found; it has to be created.

Nida’s formal equivalence (a ‘gloss translation’ keeping form and content) versus dynamic equivalence (equivalent effect). Bassnett criticizes the second through J. B. Phillips, who rendered ‘greet one another with a holy kiss’ as ‘give one another a hearty handshake all round’, and E. V. Rieu, who put Homer into prose on the grounds that prose today matches epic then. The two types can conflict.

Popovič’s ‘invariant core’ is what all translations of a work share; the variants change the form but not that core. Neubert sees equivalence as semiotic, with semantic above syntactic and pragmatic conditioning both: Italian or Spanish blasphemies may need English sexual expletives for the same shock, and letter-closing formulas differ by culture and period.

Bassnett’s advertising example: in Britain whisky is sold on tradition and quality and Martini on youthful glamour, while in Italy the images are reversed. So Scotch in Britain is functionally ‘equivalent’ to Martini in Italy. Equivalence is not sameness, which cannot exist even between two TL versions of one text.
list: Linguistic equivalence: word-for-word homogeneity.
Paradigmatic equivalence: elements of grammar.
Stylistic (translational) equivalence: functional equivalence aiming at expressive identity.
Textual (syntagmatic) equivalence: form and shape. (Popovič’s four types)

p: Too much has been written about loss and too little about gain: a translator can also enrich or clarify a text, as Wyatt and Surrey did with Petrarch. Nida’s Guaica example shows a three-way moral scheme (good, bad, violating taboo) that does not map onto English. Many languages have dense vocabularies, such as Finnish for snow, Arabic for camel behaviour and French for bread.

Catford separates linguistic untranslatability (no TL structure, though restructuring usually solves it: Danish Jeg fandt brevet → I found the letter) from cultural untranslatability (no matching situational feature: a Finnish or Japanese ‘bathroom’). Bassnett argues that ‘home’ and ‘democracy’ are just as culture-bound: compare the American Democratic Party, the German Democratic Republic and the democratic wing of the British Conservatives. Since language is culture’s primary modelling system, cultural untranslatability is part of every translation.

Popovič’s second type covers cases where the relation between the writer and the expression has no match: Danish Tak for mad (thanks to the host after a meal), Italian tamponamento (a minor car bump, loaded with Italian driving culture). Mounin’s balance: communication through translation is never complete, and so never wholly impossible. Levý’s ‘minimax’: in practice the translator picks the solution with maximum effect for minimum effort.

Venuti (The Translator’s Invisibility, 1995): Anglo-American culture prizes fluent translations that hide their foreign origin, which makes translators invisible and reflects ‘anglocentric complacency’. He used publication figures to show how little is translated into English, and urged translation as ‘a locus of difference’.

Building on Schleiermacher (1813), Venuti prefers foreignization, which stretches the target language, to domestication (acculturation), which makes a text read as if written in the TL. In The Scandals of Translation (1998) he treats the choice as an ethical one.

Lefevere (1992): most readers meet literature ‘rewritten by its rewriters’. Translation sits with historiography, anthologies, criticism, editing and film adaptation as forms of rewriting, and belongs at the centre of literary and cultural studies.

Theory explains the process; it does not prescribe a perfect translation. The translator is both receiver and emitter: Author – Text – Receiver = Translator – Text – Receiver. Octavio Paz: every text is a translation of a translation, and every translation is also unique.

sections.h: Why history matters, and the trouble with periods
p: The study of translation over time is a vital part of literary and cultural history. The word-for-word versus sense-for-sense debate began in Rome and never ended. Bible translators were persecuted while scholars freely retranslated the classics. The Romantics’ hermeneutic approach reflects new ideas of the individual.

George Steiner (After Babel) proposes four periods: (1) from Cicero and Horace to Tytler (1791), empirical, theory drawn from practice; (2) to Larbaud (1946), theory and hermeneutics; (3) from the 1940s, machine translation, structural linguistics and communication theory; (4) from the 1960s, a return to hermeneutic, almost metaphysical inquiry. Bassnett notes how lopsided this is (1,700 years against 30) and, following Lotman, prefers to trace lines of approach rather than fixed periods.

The Romans saw themselves as continuing the Greeks; their literary system ranked texts and authors across languages. Cicero: ‘If I render word for word, the result will sound uncouth, and if … I alter anything … I shall seem to have departed from the function of a translator.’ Horace warned against rendering ‘word for word like a slavish translator’, and compared new and dying words to leaves in spring and autumn.

The principle was non verbum de verbo, sed sensum exprimere de sensu: not word for word but sense for sense, with responsibility to the TL reader. Because educated Romans read Greek, a translation was read alongside the original as a metatext, almost an exercise in comparative stylistics. Longinus counts imitation and emulation of the great writers as a path to the sublime.

The history of Bible translation is western cultural history in miniature. St Jerome (commissioned in 384) followed Cicero and translated sense for sense, but the line between stylistic licence and heresy stayed dangerous for centuries. Translation became a weapon in religious and political conflict as nation states rose and Latin declined.

The Wycliffite Bible (1380–84), revised by John Purvey, aimed to be plain to lay readers: translate ‘after the sentence’ (meaning), ‘as open or opener in English as in Latin’. Its Prologue describes four stages: establish the source text, compare versions, consult ‘old grammarians and old divines’, then translate the meaning clearly and have it checked. Tyndale’s New Testament (1525) followed; he was burned at the stake in 1536. Erasmus wished the ploughman would sing scripture at his plough.

Luther (Circular Letter on Translation, 1530) used übersetzen and verdeutschen (to Germanize) almost interchangeably: ‘the grammar shall not rule over the meaning’. The King James preface asks: ‘is the kingdom of God words or syllables?’
list: Correct errors from faulty manuscripts or poor language skills.
Produce an accessible, beautiful vernacular style.
Clarify dogma, so the church could not present scripture to lay readers as a metatext. (Aims of 16th-century Bible translators)

p: Interlinear glosses, such as the 10th-century Northumbrian gloss of the Lindisfarne Gospels, were word for word but still translations. King Alfred (871–99) translated to rebuild learning after the Danish invasions, ‘sometimes word by word, sometimes sense by sense’, as function demanded, and claimed English as a literary language.

Medieval schools used translation and paraphrase (from Quintilian) as rhetorical exercises. Folena distinguishes vertical translation (from a prestige language such as Latin into the vernacular) from horizontal translation (between languages of similar standing). Since originality was not prized, the line between translating, adapting and borrowing (Chaucer) is rarely clear.

Étienne Dolet was executed for heresy (1546) after a ‘mistranslation’ of Plato implying disbelief in immortality. His La manière de bien traduire (1540) gave five ranked principles. George Chapman, translator of Homer, asked the translator to avoid word for word, reach the ‘spirit’ of the original, and avoid over-loose translation by studying other versions and glosses.
list: Fully understand the sense and meaning of the original (you may clarify obscurities).
Know both SL and TL perfectly.
Avoid word-for-word renderings.
Use forms of speech in common use.
Choose and order words to produce the right tone. (Dolet, 1540)

p: ‘The Reformation was primarily a dispute between translators’ (Cary). Translators affirmed their own time through current idiom: North’s Plutarch (1579) turns indirect speech into direct and uses phrases like ‘not in hugger mugger’. Wyatt’s Petrarch is faithful to the poem’s function for its readers rather than to its words. Philemon Holland made patres et plebs ‘Lords and Commons’ and the praetor a ‘Lord Chiefe Justice’, and boasted of subduing Roman literature ‘under the dent of the English pen’.
Steiner: translation was ‘the matière première of the imagination’. It was a primary activity, and the translator at times looks more like an activist than a servant.

sections.h: The seventeenth century: Denham, Cowley, Dryden
p: Denham: translate ‘Poesie into Poesie’; poetry evaporates in the pouring, and ‘if a new spirit be not added in the transfusion, there will remain nothing but a Caput mortuum’. Cowley openly ‘took, left out and added’ what he pleased, aiming at the author’s ‘way and manner of speaking’.

Dryden (Preface to Ovid’s Epistles, 1680) set three types and chose the middle way, on condition that the translator is a poet, masters both languages and understands the author’s spirit. Like a portrait painter, the translator must make the likeness resemble the original. In his Aeneid he wanted ‘to make Virgil speak such English as he would himself have spoken, if he had been born in England, and in this present age.’ Pope followed the same middle ground, keeping alive the ‘fire’ of the poem.
list: Metaphrase: word by word and line by line.
Paraphrase: translation with latitude, sense for sense.
Imitation: the translator may abandon the text as he sees fit.

sections.h: The eighteenth century: Johnson, Goethe, Tytler
p: The translator had a moral duty to the contemporary reader, which led to large rewritings (Shakespeare, Racine). Dr Johnson: added elegance is welcome if nothing is lost, for ‘the purpose of a writer is to be read’. Pope’s Andromache faints in Latinate grandeur; Chapman’s is a warrior, ‘black night strook through her’.

Goethe’s three recurring phases: (1) meeting the foreign on our own terms (Luther’s Bible); (2) appropriation, absorbing the sense and reproducing it in our own terms (Wieland, the French manner); (3) the highest, aiming at identity between SL and TL through a new manner that fuses the original’s uniqueness with a new form (Voss’s Homer). This edges towards untranslatability.

Tytler’s Essay on the Principles of Translation (1791) was the first systematic study in English. He reacted against loose paraphrase, but let the translator clarify obscurities, and kept the painter image: the translator cannot use the same colours but must give the picture ‘the same force and effect’.
list: Give a complete transcript of the ideas of the original.
Keep the style and manner of the original.
Have all the ease of original composition. (Tytler, 1791)

p: Romanticism rejected rationalism and exalted the creative Imagination. Coleridge set Imagination against mechanical Fancy, and A. W. Schlegel set organic against mechanical form. Schlegel held that all speaking and writing is translation, yet kept Dante’s terza rima; Friedrich Schlegel saw translation as a category of thought. A flood of translations followed (Schlegel–Tieck’s Shakespeare, Cary’s Dante), so many that influence study and translation study blurred.

If poetry lies beneath and between the words, the translator is stuck. Shelley: ‘It were as wise to cast a violet into a crucible … as to seek to transfuse from one language into another the creations of a poet. The plant must spring again from its seed’. Two ways out: literal translation, or an artificial, strange language that conveys the feeling of the original.

Schleiermacher proposed a separate sub-language for translated literature. F. W. Newman would keep every peculiarity of the original, ‘with the greater care the more foreign it may be’. William Morris’s deliberately archaic sagas and Aeneid make no concessions: Wilde praised his Odyssey as ‘poetry into poetry’ but found its spirit more Norse than Greek.

Carlyle, Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites revered the original as a possession of beauty, but their archaic versions served a small cultivated minority, which laid the ground for translation as a minority interest. Arnold told translators to please ‘those who both know Greek and can appreciate poetry’, bringing the reader to the source, the opposite of Erasmus’s ploughman.

Longfellow cut Dante’s rhyme to keep ‘fidelity, truth – the life of the hedge itself’: ‘the business of a translator is to report what the author says, not to explain what he means’. FitzGerald’s Rubáiyát took the opposite line, preferring ‘a live sparrow than a stuffed eagle’, though in a patronizing spirit. Arnold mocked archaizers with the verb ‘to newmanize’. J. M. Cohen called mock-antique language Victorian translation’s ‘fundamental error’; Steiner and Borchardt read archaizing as an attempt to ‘colonize’ the past.
list: Translation as a scholar’s activity, assuming the source is superior.
Translation as a way to send the intelligent reader back to the original.
Translation that makes the reader the equal of Schleiermacher’s ‘better reader’ through deliberate foreignness.
The translator, ‘like Aladdin in the enchanted vaults’, offering a personal choice.
Translation to ‘upgrade’ a source seen as culturally lower. (Five Victorian types)

p: English-language discussion long kept Victorian habits (literalness, archaizing, pedantry, second-rate texts for an elite) and argued about evaluation without theory. Exceptions include Ezra Pound, Belloc’s lecture On Translation (1931) and James McFarlane’s ‘Modes of Translation’ (1953), the first modern interdisciplinary programme in the West.

Steiner’s short list of those who said anything new: Jerome, Luther, Dryden, Hölderlin, Novalis, Schleiermacher, Nietzsche, Pound, Valéry, MacKenna, Rosenzweig, Benjamin, Quine. Bassnett’s point: ideas about translation belong to the age and the socio-economic forces that produce them.

sections.h: Coming of age: skopos, power, the Internet
p: Two lines emerged late in the century: translation as an intercultural transaction shaped by power (postcolonial, cultural and gender studies; Derrida, Bourdieu, Bhabha, Spivak), and functionalism, which sets equivalence aside for the text’s purpose (Vermeer, Reiss, Nord).

Skopos (Greek ‘purpose’; Reiss & Vermeer, 1984; Nord, 1997): decide what the text must do and translate to that end, from word for word to full restructuring, adding or deleting as needed. Vermeer: translate ‘in a way that enables your text/translation to function in the situation in which it is used’. Gentzler says it ‘breaks the two thousand year-old chain’ of faithful versus free. It leans towards domestication.

Translation and power: Even-Zohar (1978) argued that cultures translate according to need, with young or unsettled literatures translating more, established ones less (hence few translations into English today). Bassnett and Lefevere’s ‘cultural turn’ (1990): translation is never innocent. Tymoczko and Gentzler: translators ‘participate in the powerful acts that create knowledge and shape culture’.

The Internet brought translation memories, corpora, 24-hour news and website localization (Pym), where much content is barely read. Audiovisual and technological translation now needs to be a field in its own right, beyond the old debates.

Theory without practice is like driving a Rolls without knowing how it moves; practice without theory is the mechanic who never takes the car out. Cluysenaar: do not work from general rules but from ‘a description of the dominant structure of every individual work’. A text is a set of systems within other systems.

The translator is first a reader, and reading means taking a position. Belitt’s Neruda gives the play an ‘American sound’ and turns its politics into a cowboys-and-Indians myth (an extreme case of the third reader position). Meaning drifts over time: when Gloucester calls Regan ‘Naughty lady’ before his blinding, the word was far heavier than it is today.

Barthes makes the reader a producer of the text, and Kristeva’s intertextuality links every text to others, so there is no single ‘correct’ reading. That freedom must be used responsibly: missing Brecht’s politics or Shakespeare’s irony treats the original as your own property. It is foolish to say the translator should translate but not interpret; the two cannot be separated. How much form, metre and register to keep depends on the TL system and the purpose (a Loeb facing-page crib differs from a version for readers who know nothing of the source).
list: Reads for content only, the prose argument (inadequate for translation).
Grasps how the levels of the work interact (the ideal starting point).
Deliberately extracts one level for a purpose.
Finds elements that were not part of the text’s genesis and uses them (almost unavoidable with distant texts). (Lotman’s four reader positions)

p: Lefevere studied English versions of Catullus 64 and listed seven strategies. Each fails in the same way: it puts one element of the poem above the whole. Popovič: the translator ‘has the right to differ organically, to be independent’, as long as it is for the sake of the original. Pound kept ‘Oetian gods’ because the singular would ‘bitch the movement of the verse’, and said his Homage to Propertius was not a translation but a resurrection.

Three versions of Catullus 13 (the dinner invitation) share Popovič’s invariant core: the invitation, the joking affection, the plea of poverty. Marris (1924) keeps rhyme and metre but blurs the sense and shifts register. Copley (1957) turns it into an American wisecracking monologue (‘VENUS and CUPID LTD.’), closer in spirit but too low in register for an aristocratic poet, and already dated. Ben Jonson’s ‘Inviting a friend to supper’ is not a close translation, yet comes nearest in mood: Jakobson’s creative transposition.

Two Seafarers. Pound’s is free verse, mock-Germanic, sound-driven and stripped of Christian meaning (mid englum, ‘among the angels’, becomes ‘’mid the English’). Kennedy’s keeps half-lines and regular stress, mixes in modern words (‘landlubber’) and stops at line 65, a restless Ulysses figure. Both start from the source and build poems of their own; every reading is an interpretation.

Ungaretti’s ‘Vallone, 20 April 1917’ in two versions. Creagh normalizes the syntax (6 lines, ‘adrift in infinite space’); Tomlinson keeps ‘frozen’ on its own line with Italian word order and the Latinate ‘abandoned in the infinite’. In free verse, layout is meaning, and Ungaretti’s simplicity is a form of ostranenie (making strange).

Petrarch’s sonnet ‘Amor, che nel penser mio vive e regna’ in Wyatt and Surrey. Wyatt’s lover becomes active and loyal, battle turns to pageantry, ‘For goode is the liff, ending faithfully’. Surrey makes Love a coward and his lover ‘fawtless’, and builds three quatrains and a final couplet. Keeping the form brought the sonnet into English, while the meanings were reshaped for a society that prized upward mobility.
list: Phonemic translation: reproduces the SL sounds; clumsy, often senseless.
Literal translation: word for word; distorts sense and syntax.
Metrical translation: keeps the metre at the expense of the whole.
Poetry into prose: distorts sense and communicative value, though less badly.
Rhymed translation: ‘double bondage’ of metre and rhyme; a caricature.
Blank verse translation: more accurate, but bound by the chosen structure.
Interpretation: versions (same substance, new form) and imitations (a new poem sharing only the title and starting point). (Lefevere’s seven strategies)
sections.note: There is no single right way to translate a poem, just as there is no single right way to write one. The original is fixed; translations, like readings, are endless.

p: Prose gets less attention because people wrongly assume a novel is simpler than a poem. Bassnett’s students often begin translating a novel they have not read, something nobody would do with a poem.

Lowe-Porter’s Magic Mountain opening is brisk and readable but flattens Mann. It merges sentences, drops ‘zu Schiff’ (by boat), turns the classical Gestade into plain names, characterizes the hero (‘unassuming’ for einfacher, ‘ordinary’) and mistranslates Schlünde (abysses) as ‘marshes’. Mann’s journey works on several levels at once: literal, national, and the reader’s quest.

Silone’s Fontamara opens with five carefully patterned sentences (time phrases, verbs of movement, repetition) in a quietly ironic tone. The English reshuffles them, inconsistently, and loses the climax. Iser: a sentence in a novel always points beyond itself. Translating sentences at face value produces Popovič’s ‘negative shifts’: mistranslation, ‘subinterpretation’, and superficial reading of the links between sentences.

The prime unit is the whole text, but the prose translator needs working units that keep the whole in view. Translate function, not systems: Russian name variants (Vasilisa, Vasya, Vasyuk) mark point of view (Uspensky), and copying them all into English only confuses readers. Robert Adams: Paris must stay Paris and Pierre must not become Peter, but ‘I am enchanted, Madame’ sounds silly in English.
list: Do not plod word by word; ‘block out’ the work and ask what the whole sense of each section is.
Render idiom by idiom: Greek ‘By the Dog!’ is ‘By God!’; the French historic present becomes an English past.
Render intention by intention, adding words where your own idiom needs them.
Beware faux amis: demander is ‘to ask’, not ‘to demand’.
Transmute boldly: translation is ‘the resurrection of an alien thing in a native body’.
Never embellish. (Belloc’s six rules for prose, 1931)

p: A play text is incomplete until performed, so the translator must decide whether to translate it as literature or as one element in the larger system of theatre. Ubersfeld warns that treating performance as a mere ‘translation’ of a sacred written text leads to judging every director and translator as deviant. Veltruský: dialogue is bound to its situation, which shapes it and is shaped by it. Corrigan: the translator must hear the voice and the ‘gesture’ of the language. Bogatyrev: theatre speech is accompanied by gesture, costume and set, all signs of social situation.

Phèdre’s first line, ‘Le dessein en est pris; je pars, cher Théramène’, in three versions: Cairncross, ‘I have resolved, Theramenes, to go’; Lowell, ‘No, no, my friend, we’re off’; Harrison, ‘No. No. I can’t. I can’t. How can I stay?’ Only the last two carry the gestural rhythm, which Barrault said matched Hippolyte’s footsteps, landing on the name.

Ambrose Phillips’s The Distres’t Mother (Andromache) cut, added and even gave the play a happy ending, and it stayed in the repertoire through the 18th century. He worked to three criteria: playability, the stage conventions of his day, and clear relationships between characters. He broke up long monologues and turned the confidant into a real friend. Tony Harrison’s Phaedra Britannica (1976) moves the play to colonial India: ‘India put dark passions in my breast’. The taboo becomes inter-racial rather than incest, yet the scene’s movement is kept better than in Lowell’s more ‘faithful’ but I-heavy version.

The theatre translator handles linguistic, paralinguistic (pitch, intonation, pace) and gestural systems for a public audience. That justifies changes like Phillips’s and Harrison’s, made for performance.

sections.h: Continuity, contact zones and the future
p: Machine translation, film dubbing and subtitling, and interpreting were left out of the first edition. Bassnett now argues that audiovisual and digital translation need their own theories. The TV news translator, for instance, is both translator and interpreter, writing one oral text from several sources.

Two strands are converging: functionalism frees non-literary translators to adjust texts to their purpose, and the idea of the visible translator as ‘rewriter’ does the same for literature, as Pound claimed a century ago.

Translation as continuity: Walter Benjamin’s ‘The Task of the Translator’ (1923), taken up by Derrida, says a translation marks a work’s ‘survival’. Without translation we would have lost Greek epic and drama, Gilgamesh, the Mahabharata and classical Chinese poetry. Benjamin’s ‘pure language’: find in your own language ‘the latent structure which can awake an echo of the original’. Seamus Heaney looked for ‘the tuning fork’ for the music of Beowulf (1999), and both it and Ted Hughes’s Tales from Ovid (1997) became bestsellers. Stephen Harrison speaks of appropriation rather than homage.

Translation as contact zone: Spivak’s Death of a Discipline (2003); Emily Apter’s The Translation Zone (2006), prompted after 9/11 by America’s lack of translators for Middle Eastern languages; Sherry Simon’s Cities in Translation (2012); Michael Cronin’s Translation and Identity (2006); Edwin Gentzler’s Translation and Identity in the Americas (2008).

Beyond the West: Chinese scholars question whether Western models fit their traditions (Wang Ning), and Harish Trivedi notes that the Sanskrit anuvad means ‘saying after’: a temporal image, not the spatial ‘carrying across’ of translatio. A shared history of translation across cultures is needed.

Still to do: theatre translation with performance in mind, prose translation, poetry methods, texts from outside Europe and the Americas, ancient texts, self-translation, news and political discourse. Jakobson: the ‘dogma of untranslatability’ is an attempt to cut the Gordian knot, and translators go on translating.
